label: def:Pcyl
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Pcyl}
$\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{cyl}}$ is the set of pairs $(n,\omega)\in\mathbb N\times(0,\infty)$ such that no more than $n$
pairwise non-overlapping cylinders of radius $\omega$ can simultaneously touch the unit ball. We call
these \emph{cylinder-packing pairs}.

label: lem:dictionary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:dictionary}
Let $N\ge2$ and $\omega>0$. There exist $N$ pairwise non-overlapping cylinders of radius
$\omega$ touching $B$ if and only if there exist $N$ lines tangent to $\mathbb{S}^2$
with pairwise distances at least
$
\tau(\omega)=\frac{2\omega}{1+\omega}$.
head: environment

label: rem:ringTau
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ringTau}
Since $\frac{\omega_n}{1+\omega_n}=\sin\frac\pi n$, the ring of $n$ cylinders has separation
$\tau(\omega_n)=2\sin\frac\pi n$. This is the edge length of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in the unit
circle. Hence $N_{\max}(2\sin\frac\pi n)\ge n$.

label: lem:usc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:usc}
The function $g\mapsto\operatorname{dist}(\ell_0,g\cdot\ell_0)$ is upper semicontinuous on $\operatorname{SO}(3)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition
$\operatorname{dist}(\ell_0,g\cdot\ell_0)=\inf_{s,t\in\mathbb{R}}\bigl\|\overrightarrow{e_3}+t\overrightarrow{e_1}-g\cdot \overrightarrow{e_3}-s\,g\cdot \overrightarrow{e_1}\bigr\|$,
an infimum of a family of continuous functions of $g$, hence upper semicontinuous.
head: environment

label: cor:attain
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:attain}
For every integer $N\ge2$ the number
$\tau^*(N)=\sup\{\tau\in(0,2):N_{\max}(\tau)\ge N\}$
is attained, in the sense that $N_{\max}(\tau)\ge N$ holds if and only if $\tau\le\tau^*(N)$.
Consequently $R_N=\frac{\tau^*(N)}{2-\tau^*(N)}$ and $\mathcal N(\omega)\ge N$ if and only if
$\omega\le R_N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Phi(g_1,\dots,g_N)=\min_{i\ne j}\operatorname{dist}(\ell_0,g_i^{-1}g_j\cdot\ell_0)$. Each of the finitely
many entries is upper semicontinuous by Lemma~\ref{lem:usc}, and a minimum of finitely many
upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. As $\operatorname{SO}(3)^N$ is compact, $\Phi$ attains
its maximum, say at $(\hat g_1,\dots,\hat g_N)$. Write $\hat\tau=\Phi(\hat g_1,\dots,\hat g_N)$.

If $\tau\le\hat\tau$ then $\{\hat g_1,\dots,\hat g_N\}$ is non-overlapping for $\tau$. Its
elements are distinct because $\tau>0$ and $\operatorname{dist}(\ell_0,\ell_0)=0$. So $N_{\max}(\tau)\ge N$.
If $\tau>\hat\tau$ and $X=\{g_1,\dots,g_N\}$ were non-overlapping for $\tau$, then
$\Phi(g_1,\dots,g_N)\ge\tau>\hat\tau$, contradicting maximality. Hence $\tau^*(N)=\hat\tau$ and the
stated equivalence holds. The last assertion follows by applying the increasing bijection
\eqref{eq:tauDef}.

label: lem:OSIdentity
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Both sides of \eqref{eqn:OSIdentity} are invariant under rotations. Hence we may assume that
$\overrightarrow{p'}$, $\overrightarrow{v'}$, and $\overrightarrow{w'}$ are the coordinate vectors
$\overrightarrow{e_1}$, $\overrightarrow{e_2}$, and $\overrightarrow{e_3}$. Let
$\overrightarrow{p}=\langle p_1,p_2,p_3\rangle$, $\overrightarrow{v}=\langle v_1,v_2,v_3\rangle$, and
$\overrightarrow{w}=\langle w_1,w_2,w_3\rangle$. Then
$\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{e_2}=\langle -v_3,0,v_1\rangle$. The second coordinate of
$\overrightarrow{p}\times\overrightarrow{v}$ is $w_2=p_3v_1-p_1v_3$. Therefore
$\left(\overrightarrow{e_1}-\overrightarrow{p}\right)\cdot\left(\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{e_2}\right)=-(v_3+w_2)$.
The right-hand side of \eqref{eqn:OSIdentity} becomes
\[
(v_3-w_2)^2+(v_3+w_2)^2-2\left(v_1^2+v_3^2\right)=2w_2^2-2v_1^2.
\]
The coordinates of $\overrightarrow{e_1}$ in the orthonormal basis
$\{\overrightarrow{p},\overrightarrow{v},\overrightarrow{w}\}$ are $p_1$, $v_1$, and $w_1$. Hence
$p_1^2+v_1^2+w_1^2=1$. Since $\overrightarrow{w}$ is a unit vector, also $w_1^2+w_2^2+w_3^2=1$.
Subtracting the two equations gives $w_2^2-v_1^2=p_1^2-w_3^2$. This proves
\eqref{eqn:OSIdentity}, because $\overrightarrow{p}\cdot\overrightarrow{p'}=p_1$ and
$\overrightarrow{w}\cdot\overrightarrow{w'}=w_3$.

label: lem:OSLemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:OSLemma}
Let $\ell$ and $\ell'$ be lines tangent to the unit sphere. Let
$(\overrightarrow{p},\overrightarrow{v},\overrightarrow{w})$ and
$(\overrightarrow{p'},\overrightarrow{v'},\overrightarrow{w'})$ be their associated orthonormal systems.
If $\operatorname{dist}(\ell,\ell')\ge\sqrt2$, then $\overrightarrow{p}\cdot\overrightarrow{p'}\le0$ and
$\left|\overrightarrow{w}\cdot\overrightarrow{w'}\right|\le-\overrightarrow{p}\cdot\overrightarrow{p'}$.
The last inequality is an equality if and only if the following two conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\overrightarrow{v}\cdot\overrightarrow{w'}=\overrightarrow{w}\cdot\overrightarrow{v'}$.
\item $\ell\|\ell'$ or $\operatorname{dist}(\ell,\ell')=\sqrt2$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The points $\overrightarrow{p}$ and $\overrightarrow{p'}$ lie on $\ell$ and $\ell'$. Hence
$\left\|\overrightarrow{p}-\overrightarrow{p'}\right\|\ge\operatorname{dist}(\ell,\ell')\ge\sqrt2$. Since
$\left\|\overrightarrow{p}-\overrightarrow{p'}\right\|^2=2-2\,\overrightarrow{p}\cdot\overrightarrow{p'}$, this
means $\overrightarrow{p}\cdot\overrightarrow{p'}\le0$. If $\ell$ and $\ell'$ are not parallel, then
Lemma~\ref{lem:linedist} gives
$\left(\left(\overrightarrow{p'}-\overrightarrow{p}\right)\cdot\left(\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{v'}\right)\right)^2
=\operatorname{dist}^2(\ell,\ell')\left\|\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{v'}\right\|^2\ge2\left\|\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{v'}\right\|^2$.
If they are parallel, then $\overrightarrow{v}\times\overrightarrow{v'}=0$. In both cases the last two
terms on the right-hand side of \eqref{eqn:OSIdentity} have a non-negative sum. The sum is zero if
and only if (ii) holds. The first term is zero if and only if (i) holds. Lemma~\ref{lem:OSIdentity} now
gives $\left(\overrightarrow{w}\cdot\overrightarrow{w'}\right)^2\le\left(\overrightarrow{p}\cdot\overrightarrow{p'}\right)^2$,
with equality if and only if (i) and (ii) hold. It remains to recall that
$\overrightarrow{p}\cdot\overrightarrow{p'}\le0$.
head: environment

label: lem:Cbeta
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The lines of the first pair are parallel. The difference of their base points is
$\sqrt2\,\overrightarrow{e_1}$, which is orthogonal to $\overrightarrow{e_2}$. Hence their distance is
$\sqrt2$. The same holds for the second pair. Now take one line from each pair. Then
$\overrightarrow{e_2}\times\overrightarrow{u'}=\sin\beta\,\overrightarrow{e_3}$. The difference of the
base points has $\overrightarrow{e_3}$-coordinate $-\sqrt2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:linedist} the distance
is $\sqrt2$ when $\sin\beta\neq0$. For $\beta=0$ all four lines are parallel to
$\overrightarrow{e_2}$, and their points of tangency form a square.
head: environment

label: thm:OSequality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:OSequality}
Let $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, $\ell_3$, $\ell_4$ be lines tangent to the unit sphere. Their pairwise
distances are at least $\sqrt2$ if and only if, after a rotation, they form $\mathcal C_\beta$ for
some $\beta\in[0,\pi)$.
head: environment

label: eqn:OSchain
title: Proof
body_md:
The configurations $\mathcal C_\beta$ have the required distances by Lemma~\ref{lem:Cbeta}.
Conversely, assume that the pairwise distances are at least $\sqrt2$.
For each $i$ let
$\left(\overrightarrow{p_i},\overrightarrow{v_i},\overrightarrow{w_i}\right)$ be an associated
orthonormal system. Let $P$ and $W$ be the Gram matrices with entries
$P_{ij}=\overrightarrow{p_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{p_j}$ and $W_{ij}=\overrightarrow{w_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_j}$.
Four vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are linearly dependent. Hence there is a non-zero vector
$\overrightarrow{a}\in\mathbb{R}^4$ with $\sum_ia_i\overrightarrow{w_i}=0$. Reversing the direction of $\ell_i$
does not change the line, and it replaces $\overrightarrow{w_i}$ by $-\overrightarrow{w_i}$. We
reverse every line with $a_i<0$, and we replace each such $a_i$ by $-a_i$. The relation
$\sum_ia_i\overrightarrow{w_i}=0$ still holds, and now $a_i\ge0$ for all $i$. Lemma~\ref{lem:OSLemma}
gives
\begin{align}
0&=\left\|\sum_{i}a_i\overrightarrow{w_i}\right\|^2
=\sum_{i}a_i^2+\sum_{i\neq j}W_{ij}a_ia_j
\ge\sum_{i}a_i^2-\sum_{i\neq j}\left|W_{ij}\right|a_ia_j\nonumber\\
&\ge\sum_{i}a_i^2+\sum_{i\neq j}P_{ij}a_ia_j
=\left\|\sum_{i}a_i\overrightarrow{p_i}\right\|^2\ge0.
\label{eqn:OSchain}
\end{align}
Hence all inequalities in \eqref{eqn:OSchain} are equalities.

Let us prove the following claim:
\begin{align} & \text{The matrices }W\text{ and }P\text{ are equal, or become equal after reversing one more line.} \label{eqn:ClaimInOSProof} \end{align}
The equalities in \eqref{eqn:OSchain} give $\sum_ia_i\overrightarrow{p_i}=0$. They also give
$W_{ij}=-\left|W_{ij}\right|=P_{ij}$ whenever $a_i>0$ and $a_j>0$. Now let $a_k=0$. Then
$\sum_ia_iP_{ik}=\overrightarrow{p_k}\cdot\sum_ia_i\overrightarrow{p_i}=\overrightarrow{p_k}\cdot0=0$, and all
terms $a_iP_{ik}$ are non-positive. Hence $P_{ik}=0$ whenever $a_i>0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:OSLemma} gives
$W_{ik}=0=P_{ik}$. The diagonal entries of $W$ and $P$ are all equal to $1$. So far we know that
$W_{ij}=P_{ij}$ for every pair $i\neq j$ in which at least one of $a_i$ and $a_j$ is positive. Since
$\overrightarrow{a}\neq0$ and $\overrightarrow{w_i}\neq0$, at least two of the $a_i$ are positive. Hence
there is at most one pair $(i,j)$ with $a_i=a_j=0$. If there is none, the claim
\eqref{eqn:ClaimInOSProof} is proved. Otherwise we may assume that $a_1,a_2>0$ and $a_3=a_4=0$.
Then $a_1\overrightarrow{p_1}=-a_2\overrightarrow{p_2}$. Taking lengths gives $a_1=a_2$, and hence
$\overrightarrow{p_2}=-\overrightarrow{p_1}$. In the same way $\sum_ia_i\overrightarrow{w_i}=0$ gives
$\overrightarrow{w_2}=-\overrightarrow{w_1}$. Therefore
$\overrightarrow{v_2}=\overrightarrow{w_2}\times\overrightarrow{p_2}=\overrightarrow{w_1}\times\overrightarrow{p_1}=\overrightarrow{v_1}$.
Let $k\in\{3,4\}$. We showed above that $W_{1k}=P_{1k}=0$ and $W_{2k}=P_{2k}=0$. So the inequality of
Lemma~\ref{lem:OSLemma} is an equality for the pairs $(1,k)$ and $(2,k)$, and condition (i) gives
\begin{align*}
\overrightarrow{v_1}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_k}=\overrightarrow{w_1}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_k}
=-\overrightarrow{w_2}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_k}=-\overrightarrow{v_2}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_k}
=-\overrightarrow{v_1}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_k}.
\end{align*}
Hence $\overrightarrow{v_1}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_k}=\overrightarrow{w_1}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_k}=0$. The
vector $\overrightarrow{w_1}$ is orthogonal to $\overrightarrow{v_k}$ and, since $W_{1k}=0$, also to
$\overrightarrow{w_k}$. Therefore $\overrightarrow{p_k}=\pm\overrightarrow{w_1}$. The vector
$\overrightarrow{w_k}$ is orthogonal to $\overrightarrow{v_1}$ and $\overrightarrow{w_1}$, so
$\overrightarrow{w_k}=\pm\overrightarrow{p_1}$. Then
$\overrightarrow{v_k}=\overrightarrow{w_k}\times\overrightarrow{p_k}=\pm\overrightarrow{p_1}\times\overrightarrow{w_1}=\pm\overrightarrow{v_1}$.
If $\overrightarrow{p_3}=\overrightarrow{p_4}$, then $\ell_3$ and $\ell_4$ have the same point of tangency
and parallel directions, so they coincide. Hence $P_{34}=-1$ and $W_{34}=\pm1$. Reversing $\ell_4$ if
necessary gives $W_{34}=P_{34}$. This proves the claim \eqref{eqn:ClaimInOSProof}.

From now on $W=P$. The arrays of vectors $(\overrightarrow{p_i})_{i=1}^4$ and $(\overrightarrow{w_i})_{i=1}^4$ have the
same Gram matrix. Hence the map $\sum_ix_i\overrightarrow{p_i}\mapsto\sum_ix_i\overrightarrow{w_i}$ is
well defined and preserves lengths. It extends to an orthogonal matrix $Q$ with
$Q\overrightarrow{p_i}=\overrightarrow{w_i}$ for all $i$. If $\det Q=-1$, we reverse the directions of all four lines and
replace $Q$ by $-Q$. This does not change $W$. So $Q$ is a rotation by an angle $\varphi\in[0,\pi]$ about a unit vector, which
we may take to be $\overrightarrow{e_3}$. 
The matrix representation of $Q$ is \begin{align*} Q&=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos\varphi& -\sin\varphi& 0\\ \sin\varphi&\cos\varphi&0\\0&0&1\end{array}\right].
\end{align*}
In particular $\sin\varphi\ge0$. For every unit vector $\overrightarrow{x}$ it is straightforward to verify that the quadratic form associated with $Q$ is
\begin{align*}
\overrightarrow{x}\cdot Q\overrightarrow{x}&=\cos\varphi+(1-\cos\varphi)\left(\overrightarrow{x}\cdot\overrightarrow{e_3}\right)^2.
\end{align*}

Since $\overrightarrow{p_i}\cdot Q\overrightarrow{p_i}=\overrightarrow{p_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_i}=0$,
we get $\varphi\neq0$, $\cos\varphi\le0$, and
\begin{align*}
\overrightarrow{p_i}=\left\langle r\cos\alpha_i,\ r\sin\alpha_i,\ \varepsilon_ih\right\rangle,
\quad h=\sqrt{\tfrac{-\cos\varphi}{1-\cos\varphi}},\quad r=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{1-\cos\varphi}},\quad \varepsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}.
\end{align*}
Since $W=P$ and $P_{ij}\leq 0$, all pairs satisfy $\left|W_{ij}\right|=-P_{ij}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:OSLemma},
$\overrightarrow{v_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_j}=\overrightarrow{w_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_j}$ for all
$i\neq j$. Since $\overrightarrow{v_i}=\overrightarrow{w_i}\times\overrightarrow{p_i}$ and
$\overrightarrow{v_j}=\overrightarrow{w_j}\times\overrightarrow{p_j}$, we have
\begin{align*}
\overrightarrow{v_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_j}-\overrightarrow{w_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_j}
=\det\left(\overrightarrow{w_i},\overrightarrow{p_i},\overrightarrow{w_j}\right)
-\det\left(\overrightarrow{w_i},\overrightarrow{w_j},\overrightarrow{p_j}\right)
=-\det\left(\overrightarrow{w_i},\overrightarrow{w_j},\overrightarrow{p_i}+\overrightarrow{p_j}\right).
\end{align*}
Hence the equation $\overrightarrow{v_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{w_j}=\overrightarrow{w_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{v_j}$
is equivalent to
$\det\left(\overrightarrow{w_i},\overrightarrow{w_j},\overrightarrow{p_i}+\overrightarrow{p_j}\right)=0$.
Let $\delta=\alpha_i-\alpha_j$. Since
$\overrightarrow{w_i}=Q\overrightarrow{p_i}=\left\langle r\cos(\alpha_i+\varphi),\ r\sin(\alpha_i+\varphi),\ \varepsilon_ih\right\rangle$,
expanding the determinant gives
\begin{align*}
\det\left(\overrightarrow{w_i},\overrightarrow{w_j},\overrightarrow{p_i}+\overrightarrow{p_j}\right)
&=
\begin{vmatrix}
r\cos(\alpha_i+\varphi) & r\cos(\alpha_j+\varphi) & r(\cos\alpha_i+\cos\alpha_j)\\
r\sin(\alpha_i+\varphi) & r\sin(\alpha_j+\varphi) & r(\sin\alpha_i+\sin\alpha_j)\\
\varepsilon_ih & \varepsilon_jh & (\varepsilon_i+\varepsilon_j)h
\end{vmatrix}\\
&=r^2h\cdot\begin{cases}
-2\varepsilon_i(1-\cos\varphi)\sin\delta, & \text{if }\varepsilon_i=\varepsilon_j,\\
-2\varepsilon_i\sin\varphi\,(1+\cos\delta), & \text{if }\varepsilon_i\neq\varepsilon_j.
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
Note that $r>0$ and $1-\cos\varphi>0$.
If $\cos\varphi=0$, then $h=0$. All $\overrightarrow{p_i}$ and $\overrightarrow{w_i}$ are orthogonal to
$\overrightarrow{e_3}$, so all lines are parallel to $\overrightarrow{e_3}$. The four points
$\overrightarrow{p_i}$ lie on a great circle, and their pairwise angles are at least $\frac\pi2$. Hence
consecutive points are at angle exactly $\frac\pi2$. This is the ring $\mathcal C_0$.

If $-1<\cos\varphi<0$, then $h>0$ and $\sin\varphi>0$. Take two lines at the same height. The
determinant vanishes, so $\sin\delta=0$. Also $\delta\not\equiv0\pmod{2\pi}$, since otherwise the two
lines coincide. So $\delta\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}$. Take two lines at different heights. The determinant
vanishes, so $\cos\delta=-1$. Hence every two of the four angles $\alpha_i$ differ by $\pi$ modulo
$2\pi$. This is impossible for three angles.

If $\cos\varphi=-1$, then $h=r=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ and $\sin\varphi=0$. Two lines at the same height again
satisfy $\delta\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}$. Hence each of the two circles contains exactly two of the points
$\overrightarrow{p_i}$, and they are antipodal on that circle. After a rotation about
$\overrightarrow{e_3}$, the points are $\frac1{\sqrt2}\left(\pm\overrightarrow{e_1}+\overrightarrow{e_3}\right)$
and $\frac1{\sqrt2}\left(\pm\overrightarrow{u}-\overrightarrow{e_3}\right)$. Here $Q$ is the rotation by
$\pi$ about $\overrightarrow{e_3}$. For $\overrightarrow{x}=\langle x_1,x_2,x_3\rangle$ we get
$Q\overrightarrow{x}\times\overrightarrow{x}=2x_3\left\langle-x_2,x_1,0\right\rangle$. So the directions
are $\pm\overrightarrow{e_2}$ and $\pm\overrightarrow{u'}$. This is $\mathcal C_\beta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that four non-overlapping cylinders of radius $\omega'>1+\sqrt2$ touch the unit ball. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:dictionary} there are four tangent lines with pairwise distances at least
$\tau(\omega')>\sqrt2$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:OSequality} they form a configuration $\mathcal C_\beta$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:Cbeta} two of them are at distance exactly $\sqrt2$. This is a contradiction.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The homothety of Lemma~\ref{lem:dictionary} maps configurations of cylinders bijectively to
configurations of tangent lines. Hence Theorem~\ref{thm:OSequality} proves the conjecture of
Ogievetsky and Shlosman \cite{OSsix,OSPlatonic} and \cite[Section~3.1]{OSMorse} in full. They conjectured that the four-cylinder configurations of radius
$1+\sqrt2$ form a circle modulo rotations, and that no configuration of larger radius exists. The
family $\mathcal C_\beta$ is the motion found in \cite[Section~6.3]{OSsix}. One parallel pair stays
fixed and the other pair rotates about the common perpendicular $\overrightarrow{e_3}$. As $\beta\to\pi$, the configuration
$\mathcal C_\beta$ tends to $\mathcal C_0$. Measure the angle from the direction of the first
pair to the direction of the second pair about the axis that joins the pairs. This angle is $\beta$,
and it does not change under rotations. Hence distinct $\beta\in[0,\pi)$ give configurations that are not rotations of
each other, and the family is a circle.
head: environment

label: rem:five
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:five}
The ring of five cylinders can be expanded. A numerical configuration with this property was found
by Firsching \cite{F}. The standalone verifier \cite{MRVer} confirms it in exact arithmetic for a
rational configuration of five tangent lines (Appendix~\ref{app:data}).

label: lem:distances
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eqn:distanceFormula
title: Proof
body_md:
If $\overrightarrow{v_1}$ and $\overrightarrow{v_2}^{\pm}$ are not parallel, then
\begin{align}
\operatorname{dist}(\ell^+(0),\ell^{\pm}(\Delta))&=\frac{\left|(\overrightarrow{p_2}^{\pm}-\overrightarrow{p_1})\cdot \left(\overrightarrow{v_1}\times\overrightarrow{v_2}^{\pm}\right)\right|}
{\left\|\overrightarrow{v_1}\times\overrightarrow{v_2}^{\pm}\right\|}. \label{eqn:distanceFormula}
\end{align}
Write $\overrightarrow{v_1}\times\overrightarrow{v_2}^{\pm}=\langle N_x^{\pm},N_y^{\pm},N_z^{\pm}\rangle$.
From \eqref{eqn:vectorV2P}--\eqref{eqn:vectorV2M},
\begin{align*}
N_x^{\pm}&=\left(\sin\delta(1-\cos\Delta)\pm\cos\delta\sin\varphi\sin\Delta\right)\cos\delta\cos\varphi,\\
N_y^{\pm}&=\left(\cos\delta\sin\varphi(1\mp \cos\Delta)-\sin\delta\sin\Delta \right)\cos\delta\cos\varphi,\\
N_z^{\pm}&=(-1\pm1)\sin\delta\cos\delta\sin\varphi\cos\Delta+\sin\Delta\left(\sin^2\delta\pm\cos^2\delta\sin^2\varphi\right).
\end{align*}

\emph{The line $\ell^+(\Delta)$.} Here $\overrightarrow{p_2}^+-\overrightarrow{p_1}=\cos\varphi\langle\cos\Delta-1,\sin\Delta,0\rangle$, and expanding,
\begin{align*}
\left(\overrightarrow{p_2}^+-\overrightarrow{p_1}\right)\cdot\left(\overrightarrow{v_1}\times\overrightarrow{v_2}^+\right)&=
-2\cos^2\varphi\sin\delta\cos\delta(1-\cos\Delta),\\
\left\|\overrightarrow{v_1}\times\overrightarrow{v_2}^+\right\|^2&=
\left(\sin^2\delta+\cos^2\delta\sin^2\varphi\right)\\
&\quad\cdot\left(2(1-\cos\Delta)\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi+\sin^2\Delta\left(\sin^2\delta+\cos^2\delta\sin^2\varphi\right)\right).
\end{align*}
For $\Delta\in(0,2\pi)$ the norm is positive, since its second factor is at least
$2(1-\cos\Delta)\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi>0$, so \eqref{eqn:distanceFormula} applies. For
$\Delta=0$ the lines coincide and both sides of \eqref{eq:lemmaDistl1l2Plus} vanish. Substituting,
dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos^2\delta$, and using
$1-\cos^2\Delta=(1-\cos\Delta)(1+\cos\Delta)$, $1-\cos\Delta=2\sin^2\frac\Delta2$ and
$\cos^2\varphi+\tan^2\delta+\sin^2\varphi=1+\tan^2\delta$ gives \eqref{eq:lemmaDistl1l2Plus}. The
bracket in its denominator is at least
$1+\tan^2\delta-(\tan^2\delta+\sin^2\varphi)=\cos^2\varphi>0$.

\emph{The line $\ell^-(\Delta)$.} Here
$\overrightarrow{p_2}^--\overrightarrow{p_1}=\langle\cos\varphi(\cos\Delta-1),\cos\varphi\sin\Delta,-2\sin\varphi\rangle$.
With the abbreviations
\begin{align}
A&=\sin\varphi\cos\delta\cos\tfrac{\Delta}{2}-\sin\delta\sin\tfrac{\Delta}{2},\nonumber\\
B&=\sin\delta\sin\varphi\cos\tfrac{\Delta}{2}+\cos\delta\sin\tfrac{\Delta}{2},\label{eqn:defA}\\
C&=\sin\varphi\cos\delta\sin\tfrac{\Delta}{2}+\sin\delta\cos\tfrac{\Delta}{2},\nonumber
\end{align}
a direct expansion, using the half-angle formulas, gives
\begin{align}\label{eqn:NormMinusFinal}
\left(\overrightarrow{p_2}^--\overrightarrow{p_1}\right)\cdot\left(\overrightarrow{v_1}\times\overrightarrow{v_2}^-\right)=4AB,\quad
N_z^-=-2AC,\quad (N_x^-)^2+(N_y^-)^2=4\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi\,A^2,
\end{align}
so $\|\overrightarrow{v_1}\times\overrightarrow{v_2}^-\|^2=4A^2\left[\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi+C^2\right]$.
The mixed terms in $A^2+C^2$ cancel, whence
\begin{align}\label{eqn:identityAC}
A^2+C^2=\sin^2\varphi\cos^2\delta+\sin^2\delta,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi+A^2+C^2=1.
\end{align}
In particular $\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi+C^2\ge\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi>0$, and the two direction
vectors are parallel if and only if $A=0$.

If $A\ne0$, then \eqref{eqn:distanceFormula} and \eqref{eqn:NormMinusFinal} give
\begin{align}\label{eqn:distMinusMaster}
\operatorname{dist}^2(\ell^+(0),\ell^-(\Delta))=\frac{4B^2}{\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi+C^2}.
\end{align}
For $\Delta=\pi$ (where $A=-\sin\delta\ne0$) we have $B=\cos\delta$, $C=\sin\varphi\cos\delta$, and
\eqref{eqn:distMinusMaster} equals $4$, proving the last claim. For $\Delta\ne\pi$, dividing
numerator and denominator of \eqref{eqn:distMinusMaster} by $\cos^2\delta\cos^2\frac\Delta2>0$ and
using $\tan^2\delta=\cos^2\varphi\tan^2\delta+\sin^2\varphi\tan^2\delta$ turns the denominator into
$\cos^2\varphi(1+\tan^2\delta)+(\sin\varphi\tan\delta+\tan\frac\Delta2)^2$, which is
\eqref{eq:lemmaDistl1l2Minus}.

If $A=0$, the parallel unit vectors $\overrightarrow{v_1},\overrightarrow{v_2}^-$ have the same
positive third coordinate $\cos\delta\cos\varphi$, so they are equal. Moreover
$(\overrightarrow{p_2}^--\overrightarrow{p_1})\cdot\overrightarrow{v_1}=-2\cos\varphi\cos\frac\Delta2\,A=0$,
so the distance between the two parallel lines is
$\|\overrightarrow{p_2}^--\overrightarrow{p_1}\|$, whose square
$2\cos^2\varphi(1-\cos\Delta)+4\sin^2\varphi=4(A^2+B^2)=4B^2$ agrees with
\eqref{eqn:distMinusMaster}, since \eqref{eqn:identityAC} with $A=0$ gives
$\cos^2\delta\cos^2\varphi+C^2=1$. Finally $A=0$ forces
$\tan\frac\Delta2=\sin\varphi\cot\delta>0$, so $\Delta\ne\pi$ and the reduction to
\eqref{eq:lemmaDistl1l2Minus} applies verbatim.

label: lem:arc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:arc}
Let $\tau^*=2\sin\theta$ with $\theta\in(0,\frac\pi2)$, and set
\begin{align}\label{eq:ustar}
u^*=\sqrt{c_0}\,\frac{\tau^*}{\sqrt{4-\tau^{*2}}}=\sqrt{c_0}\,\tan\theta .
\end{align}
Let
\[
J=\Bigl(2\arctan(-ST-u^*),\ 2\arctan(-ST+u^*)\Bigr).
\]
Then for $\Delta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ we have $D_{\mathrm{cross}}(\Delta)<\tau^*$ if and only if $\Delta\in J$. The
open interval $J$ has length
\[
|J|=2\bigl[\arctan(ST+u^*)-\arctan(ST-u^*)\bigr].
\]
Let
\begin{align}\label{eq:kappa}
\psi^*=\tfrac\gamma2-\arctan(ST-u^*)-\arctan(ST+u^*).
\end{align}
If $|J|\le\gamma$ and $\psi=\psi^*$, then the lattice \eqref{eq:lattice} is disjoint from $J$.
Hence every cross-group distance in $P(N;\varphi,\delta,\psi^*)$ is at least $\tau^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The function $t\mapsto\frac{2t}{\sqrt{t^2+c_0}}$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and
$u^*$ of \eqref{eq:ustar} is the value at which it equals $\tau^*$. Hence
$D_{\mathrm{cross}}(\Delta)<\tau^*$ if and only if $|w|<u^*$. Now $|w|<u^*$ means $\tan\frac\Delta2\in(-ST-u^*,\,-ST+u^*)$, and as
$\Delta\mapsto\tan\frac\Delta2$ is an increasing bijection from $(-\pi,\pi)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$ (and
$D_{\mathrm{cross}}(\pi)=2\ge\tau^*$), the failure set is exactly the interval $J$. By the oddness of
$\arctan$,
\[
|J|=2\bigl[\arctan(u^*-ST)+\arctan(u^*+ST)\bigr]
=2\bigl[\arctan(ST+u^*)-\arctan(ST-u^*)\bigr].
\]
The interval $J$ is centered at
$c=\arctan(-ST-u^*)+\arctan(-ST+u^*)=\psi^*-\frac\gamma2$. With $\psi=\psi^*$ the lattice
\eqref{eq:lattice} is $\{c+\frac\gamma2+j\gamma\}$, whose distance (on the circle) from the
center $c$ is at least $\frac\gamma2\ge\frac{|J|}2$. Since $J$ is open, no lattice point lies
in $J$.

label: eq:cos6
title: Proof
body_md:
For $y\ge0$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:cos6}
\cos y\ \ge\ 1-\frac{y^2}2+\frac{y^4}{24}-\frac{y^6}{720}.
\end{align}
Indeed, the difference of the two sides vanishes at $0$, its derivative
$-\sin y+y-\frac{y^3}6+\frac{y^5}{120}$ vanishes at $0$, the derivative of that,
$-\cos y+1-\frac{y^2}2+\frac{y^4}{24}$, vanishes at $0$, and its derivative
$\sin y-y+\frac{y^3}6$ is nonnegative by \ref{E:sin}. Integrating three times from $0$ gives
\eqref{eq:cos6}. Hence $4\sin^2\frac\pi n=2\bigl(1-\cos\frac{2\pi}n\bigr)\le\rho(2\pi/n)$ with
$\rho(y)=y^2-\frac{y^4}{12}+\frac{y^6}{360}$. Now
$\rho'(y)=\frac{y}{60}\bigl(y^4-20y^2+120\bigr)>0$ for $y>0$ (the quadratic in $y^2$ has
negative discriminant), so $\rho$ is increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and since $\pi<\frac{355}{113}$
we have $\frac{2\pi}n<Y_n$ and $\rho(2\pi/n)\le\rho(Y_n)=r_n$.

title: Proof

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:entrywise}
When $D_\ell=\operatorname{diag}(w^\ell_1,\dots,w^\ell_{n_\ell})$ is diagonal and $C_\ell$ is symmetric,
\[
\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell\,T^\ell(g)\Bigr)
=\sum_{i,j}\frac{(C_\ell)_{ij}}{w^\ell_j}\;T^\ell(g)_{ij},
\]
the sum of the entries of the Schur product of $C_\ell$ and $T^\ell(g)$, with the $j$-th column
weighted by $1/w^\ell_j$. In particular
$\operatorname{tr}(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell\,T^\ell(e))=\operatorname{tr}(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell)=\sum_i (C_\ell)_{ii}/w^\ell_i$.

label: thm:dbBound
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g_1,\dots,g_N$ be distinct elements of a non-overlapping set
(Definition~\ref{def:nonOverlappingX}), and put $S_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^{N}T^\ell(g_i)$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:Torth},
\[
T^\ell\bigl(g_i^{-1}g_j\bigr)=T^\ell(g_i)^{-1}T^\ell(g_j)
=D_\ell^{-1}\,T^\ell(g_i)^\top D_\ell\,T^\ell(g_j),
\]
so that, summing over all ordered pairs and using linearity and cyclicity of the trace,
\begin{align*}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell\,T^\ell\bigl(g_i^{-1}g_j\bigr)\Bigr)
&=\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell D_\ell^{-1}\,T^\ell(g_i)^\top D_\ell\,T^\ell(g_j)\Bigr)\\
&=\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(\bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell D_\ell^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(S_\ell^\top D_\ell S_\ell\bigr)\Bigr)
\;\ge\;0,
\end{align*}
since $D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell D_\ell^{-1}$ and $S_\ell^\top D_\ell S_\ell$ are congruent to $C_\ell$
and $D_\ell$, hence symmetric positive semidefinite, and for such $P,Q$ we have
$\operatorname{tr}(PQ)=\operatorname{tr}(\sqrt Q\,P\sqrt Q\,)\ge0$.

Summing over $\ell$ and separating the $N$ diagonal pairs $i=j$ (where
$T^\ell(e)=I$ gives the value $\sum_\ell\operatorname{tr}(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell)$) from the $N(N-1)$ off-diagonal
pairs (where $g_i^{-1}g_j\in\mathcal{D}$ by Definition~\ref{def:nonOverlappingX}, so each term is at most
$\operatorname{S}(\overrightarrow C)\le-1$),
\[
0\;\le\;N\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell\bigr)\;-\;N(N-1) .
\]
Dividing by $N$ gives $N-1\le\sum_\ell\operatorname{tr}(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell)$, which implies \eqref{eq:dbBound}.

label: rem:complete
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:complete}
In the deposited certificates $T^\ell_{\mathrm h}(q)$ is the matrix of the action of $R(q)$ on the
harmonic polynomials of degree $\ell$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$, in an integer orthogonal basis. The tables are
computed as in \cite{MRsix}. These actions are the irreducible representations of $\operatorname{SO}(3)$, one in
each dimension $2\ell+1$ \cite{BtD}. By Bochner's theorem \cite{Bochner}, in the form
\cite{SOV}, every continuous function of positive type on $\operatorname{SO}(3)$ has the form
$\sum_{\ell\ge0}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(F_\ell T^\ell(g)\bigr)$ with positive semidefinite matrices $F_\ell$. The
constant $-1$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:dbBound} plays the role of the term $\ell=0$. So the bound uses
all such functions of degree at most $L$. It is the Lov\'asz theta number \cite{Lovasz} of the
packing graph on $\operatorname{SO}(3)$, truncated at degree $L$.

label: lem:cover2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) By Lemma~\ref{lem:quat}(c) the entries of $R(q)$ together with $|q|^2=1$ determine
every product $q_aq_b$, i.e.\ the symmetric rank-one matrix $qq^\top$. If $qq^\top=q'q'^\top$ then,
taking any index $a$ with $q_a\ne0$ (such an index exists because $|q|=1$), the $a$-th columns give
$q_a\,q=q'_a\,q'$ with $q_a^2=(q'_a)^2$, so $q'=\pm q$.

\noindent (b) First, every $g\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ has an eigenvector corresponding to eigenvalue $1$. Indeed,
since $\det g=1$ and $g^\top g=I$,
\[
\det(g-I)=\det(g)\det(I-g^\top)=\det\bigl((I-g)^\top\bigr)=\det(I-g)=(-1)^3\det(g-I).
\]
Therefore, $\det(g-I)=0$ and there is a unit vector $\overrightarrow{n}$ with $g\overrightarrow{n}=\overrightarrow{n}$. Since $g$ is orthogonal and
fixes $\overrightarrow{n}$, it maps the plane $\overrightarrow{n}^\perp$ to itself, and its restriction there is an
orientation-preserving linear isometry of a plane, hence a rotation by some angle $\theta$. Let
$\overrightarrow{n}=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$ and set
\[q=\left(\cos\tfrac\theta2,\;n_x\sin\frac\theta2,\;n_y\sin\frac\theta2,\;n_z\sin\frac\theta2\right).\]
Clearly, $q$ is a unit quaternion. A direct computation from the definition of $R(q)$ shows
$R(q)\overrightarrow{n}=\overrightarrow{n}$ and that $R(q)$ rotates $\overrightarrow{n}^\perp$ by $\theta$ with the same orientation. Therefore,
$R(q)=g$.

label: lem:nhNhHh
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $R_{ij}$ for the entries of $R(q)$.
The vectors $g\overrightarrow{e_1}$ and $g\overrightarrow{e_3}$ are the first and the third column of $g$.
Hence
\begin{align*}
\overrightarrow{e_1}\times g\overrightarrow{e_1}&=|q|^{-2}\bigl(0,\,-R_{31},\,R_{21}\bigr),\\
g\overrightarrow{e_3}-\overrightarrow{e_3}&=|q|^{-2}\bigl(R_{13},\,R_{23},\,R_{33}-|q|^{2}\bigr),
\end{align*}
and $\bigl(g\overrightarrow{e_3}-\overrightarrow{e_3}\bigr)\times\overrightarrow{e_1}=|q|^{-2}\bigl(0,\,R_{33}-|q|^{2},\,-R_{23}\bigr)$.
From the definition of $R(q)$ in Section~\ref{subs:quaternionsBasic},
\begin{align*}
R_{21}&=2(q_1q_2+q_0q_3), & R_{23}&=2(q_2q_3-q_0q_1),\\
R_{31}&=2(q_1q_3-q_0q_2), & R_{33}-|q|^{2}&=-2\bigl(q_1^{2}+q_2^{2}\bigr).
\end{align*}
Substituting these gives \eqref{eq:NhExplicit} and \eqref{eq:HhExplicit} at once.
In \eqref{eq:NhExplicit} the cross terms $\pm8q_0q_1q_2q_3$ in $R_{21}^{2}+R_{31}^{2}$ cancel.
For \eqref{eq:nhExplicit}, the left-hand side is $|q|^{-4}\bigl(-R_{23}R_{31}+(R_{33}-|q|^{2})R_{21}\bigr)$, and
\begin{align*}
&-R_{23}R_{31}+\bigl(R_{33}-|q|^{2}\bigr)R_{21}\\
&\quad=-4\bigl(q_2q_3-q_0q_1\bigr)\bigl(q_1q_3-q_0q_2\bigr)-4\bigl(q_1^{2}+q_2^{2}\bigr)\bigl(q_1q_2+q_0q_3\bigr)\\
&\quad=-4\bigl(q_1q_2q_3^{2}-q_0q_2^{2}q_3-q_0q_1^{2}q_3+q_0^{2}q_1q_2\bigr)\\
&\qquad\ -4\bigl(q_1^{3}q_2+q_0q_1^{2}q_3+q_1q_2^{3}+q_0q_2^{2}q_3\bigr)\\
&\quad=-4q_1q_2\bigl(q_0^{2}+q_1^{2}+q_2^{2}+q_3^{2}\bigr).
\end{align*}
The four terms carrying $q_0q_3$ cancel in pairs.

label: thm:domainQ
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $g=|q|^{-2}R(q)$ and $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(\ell_0,g\cdot\ell_0)$.
The line $g\cdot\ell_0$ passes through $g\overrightarrow{e_3}$ with direction $g\overrightarrow{e_1}$.
Let $d$ be the distance from the point $g\overrightarrow{e_3}$ to the line $\ell_0$.
Since $\overrightarrow{e_1}$ is a unit vector, $d=\bigl\|\bigl(g\overrightarrow{e_3}-\overrightarrow{e_3}\bigr)\times\overrightarrow{e_1}\bigr\|$.
By \eqref{eq:HhExplicit} and \eqref{eq:Uh}, $U_{\mathrm h}(q)=B|q|^{4}\bigl(d^{2}-\tau^{2}\bigr)$.
So $U_{\mathrm h}(q)\ge0$ holds exactly when $d\ge\tau$.
Also $\delta\le d$, because $g\overrightarrow{e_3}$ lies on $g\cdot\ell_0$.

\emph{Case $\bigl(q_0^{2}+q_1^{2}\bigr)\bigl(q_2^{2}+q_3^{2}\bigr)>0$.}
By \eqref{eq:NhExplicit}, $\overrightarrow{e_1}\times g\overrightarrow{e_1}\ne0$, so the lines are not parallel.
Lemma~\ref{lem:linedist} with $\overrightarrow{p_1}=\overrightarrow{e_3}$, $\overrightarrow{v_1}=\overrightarrow{e_1}$,
$\overrightarrow{p_2}=g\overrightarrow{e_3}$ and $\overrightarrow{v_2}=g\overrightarrow{e_1}$, together with
\eqref{eq:NhExplicit} and \eqref{eq:nhExplicit}, gives
\[
\delta^{2}=\frac{4\,q_1^{2}q_2^{2}}{\bigl(q_0^{2}+q_1^{2}\bigr)\bigl(q_2^{2}+q_3^{2}\bigr)} .
\]
Hence $Q_{\mathrm h}(q)=B\bigl(q_0^{2}+q_1^{2}\bigr)\bigl(q_2^{2}+q_3^{2}\bigr)\bigl(\delta^{2}-\tau^{2}\bigr)$.
So $Q_{\mathrm h}(q)\ge0$ holds exactly when $\delta\ge\tau$.
In that case $d\ge\delta\ge\tau$, so $U_{\mathrm h}(q)\ge0$ automatically.

\emph{Case $\bigl(q_0^{2}+q_1^{2}\bigr)\bigl(q_2^{2}+q_3^{2}\bigr)=0$.}
Then $q_0=q_1=0$ or $q_2=q_3=0$. In both cases $q_1q_2=0$, so $Q_{\mathrm h}(q)=0$.
By \eqref{eq:NhExplicit} the lines are parallel.
So $\delta=d$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:linedist}, and $\delta\ge\tau$ holds exactly when $U_{\mathrm h}(q)\ge0$.

label: thm:certificate
title: Theorem

\label{thm:certificate}
If a certificate at $(\tau,L,T^{*})$ exists, then
\[
N_{\max}(\tau)\;\le\;1+\left\lfloor T^{*}\right\rfloor .

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: $T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}$ descends to a map on $\operatorname{SO}(3)$.} For $g\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ choose, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cover2}(b), a unit quaternion $q$ with $R(q)=g$, and set
$T^{\ell}(g)=T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}(q)$. This is well defined: by Lemma~\ref{lem:cover2}(a) the only
other choice is $-q$, and by \ref{H:hom} the entries of $T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}$ are homogeneous of the
even degree $2\ell$, so $T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}(-q)=T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}(q)$.

\emph{Step 2: the hypotheses of Section~\ref{sec:DBSequence}.} Each $D_\ell$ is diagonal with
positive entries, hence symmetric positive definite. Let $g_1,g_2\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ and pick unit
quaternions $q^{(1)},q^{(2)}$ with $R(q^{(i)})=g_i$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:quat}(b),
$R(q^{(1)}*q^{(2)})=g_1g_2$ and $|q^{(1)}*q^{(2)}|=1$, so \ref{H:mult} gives
\begin{align*}
T^{\ell}(g_1g_2)=T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}\bigl(q^{(1)}*q^{(2)}\bigr)
=T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}(q^{(1)})\,T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h}(q^{(2)})=T^{\ell}(g_1)T^{\ell}(g_2),
\end{align*}
and \ref{H:orth} at a unit quaternion gives
$T^{\ell}(g)^{\top}D_\ell T^{\ell}(g)=D_\ell$. Thus the data $(D_\ell,T^{\ell})_{\ell=1}^{L}$ satisfy
(i)--(ii) of Section~\ref{sec:DBSequence}, and by \ref{H:psd} the sequence
$\overrightarrow C=(C_\ell)_{\ell=1}^{L}$ is admissible in Definition~\ref{def:DB}.

\emph{Step 3: $P$ computes the two-point sum.} For a unit quaternion $q$ we have
$|q|^{2}=1$, so by \eqref{eq:P} and Remark~\ref{rem:entrywise},
\begin{align*}
P(q)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{i,j}\frac{(C_\ell)_{ij}(T^{\ell}_{\mathrm h})_{ij}(q)}{w^{\ell}_j}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell\,T^{\ell}\bigl(R(q)\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{align*}
By \ref{H:hom} the $\ell$-th summand of \eqref{eq:P} is homogeneous of degree
$2(L-\ell)+2\ell=2L$, so $P$ is homogeneous of degree $2L$. Hence for arbitrary $q\ne0$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:PisF}
\frac{P(q)}{\bigl(|q|^{2}\bigr)^{L}}
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell\,T^{\ell}\bigl(|q|^{-2}R(q)\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{align}

\emph{Step 4: \ref{H:cover} is exactly $\operatorname{S}(\overrightarrow C)\le-1$.} Let $g\in\mathcal{D}(\tau)$ and
pick $q\ne0$ with $g=|q|^{-2}R(q)$. By \eqref{eq:Kdef} we have $q\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm h}(\tau)$, so
\ref{H:cover} gives $G(q)\ge0$, i.e.\ $P(q)\le-(|q|^{2})^{L}$. Dividing by $(|q|^{2})^{L}>0$ and
using \eqref{eq:PisF},
\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\operatorname{tr}\!\Bigl(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell\,T^{\ell}(g)\Bigr)\;\le\;-1 .
\]
Taking the supremum over $g\in\mathcal{D}(\tau)$ yields $\operatorname{S}(\overrightarrow C)\le-1$.

\emph{Step 5: conclusion.} By \ref{H:trace} and Theorem~\ref{thm:dbBound},
\begin{align*}
N_{\max}(\tau)\le1+\left\lfloor\sum_{\ell}\operatorname{tr}(D_\ell^{-1}C_\ell)\right\rfloor
=1+\left\lfloor T^{*}\right\rfloor. \qedhere
\end{align*}

10-2\sqrt5\ge\frac{1447209}{262144}
\iff 1174231\ge 524288\sqrt5
\iff 1174231^2\ge5\cdot524288^2.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Using $|v_iv_j|\le\tfrac12(v_i^{2}+v_j^{2})$ and then the symmetry of $E$,
\begin{align*}
\Bigl|\sum_{i\ne j}E_{ij}v_iv_j\Bigr|
\;\le\;\sum_{i\ne j}|E_{ij}|\,\tfrac12\bigl(v_i^{2}+v_j^{2}\bigr)
\;=\;\sum_{i}v_i^{2}\sum_{j\ne i}|E_{ij}|
\;\le\;\sum_{i}E_{ii}v_i^{2},
\end{align*}
so $v^{\top}Ev=\sum_i E_{ii}v_i^{2}+\sum_{i\ne j}E_{ij}v_iv_j\ge0$.

label: prop:psd
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:psd}
Write $\widehat C_\ell=2^{\kappa}C_\ell$ for the deposited integer matrix, where $\kappa$ is the
even integer deposited as \texttt{cDenLog2}, and let $S_\ell$ and
$W_\ell$ be the deposited positive integer scalar and integer matrix. If
\[
E_\ell\;=\;S_\ell\,\widehat C_\ell\;-\;W_\ell^{\top}W_\ell
\]
is symmetric and diagonally dominant, in the sense that
$(E_\ell)_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|(E_\ell)_{ij}|$ for every $i$, then $C_\ell$ is symmetric positive
semidefinite.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{lem:domPSD}, $E_\ell\succeq0$. Also $W_\ell^{\top}W_\ell\succeq0$, since
$v^{\top}W_\ell^{\top}W_\ell v=\|W_\ell v\|^{2}\ge0$ for every $v$. Hence
\[
2^{\kappa}S_\ell\,C_\ell\;=\;S_\ell\,\widehat C_\ell\;=\;E_\ell+W_\ell^{\top}W_\ell\;\succeq\;0,
\]
and dividing by the positive scalar $2^{\kappa}S_\ell$ gives $C_\ell\succeq0$. Symmetry of $C_\ell$ is
symmetry of the deposited $\widehat C_\ell$.

label: lem:gram
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:gram}
Let $\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{n_d\times n_d}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, and define
\[
\sigma(q)\;=\;\mathfrak m_d(q)^{\top}\,\Sigma\,\mathfrak m_d(q).
\]
Then $\sigma$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2d$ and $\sigma(q)\ge0$ for every
$q\in\mathbb{R}^{4}$. Moreover $\sigma$ is a sum of squares of forms of degree $d$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each entry of $\mathfrak m_d(q)\mathfrak m_d(q)^{\top}$ is a monomial of degree $2d$, so $\sigma$
is a form of degree $2d$. For fixed $q$ the number $\sigma(q)=v^{\top}\Sigma v$ with
$v=\mathfrak m_d(q)$ is non-negative because $\Sigma\succeq0$. For the last statement, write
$\Sigma=W^{\top}W$, for instance from the spectral decomposition. Then
$\sigma(q)=\|W\mathfrak m_d(q)\|^{2}$ is the sum of the squares of the forms $\bigl(W\mathfrak
m_d(q)\bigr)_i$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{E:sin}: $f(x)=\sin x-x+\frac{x^3}6$ has $f(0)=0$ and $f'(x)=\cos x-1+\frac{x^2}2\ge0$,
since $g(x)=\cos x-1+\frac{x^2}2$ has $g(0)=0$ and $g'(x)=x-\sin x\ge0$. The upper bound is
standard.

\ref{E:tan}: $\frac{\tan y}y$ is increasing on $(0,\frac\pi2)$ because
$(y\sec^2y-\tan y)=\frac{y-\sin y\cos y}{\cos^2y}>0$. Hence for $y\in(0,1]$,
$\tan y\le y\tan1<y\sqrt3$, using $1<\frac\pi3$ and the monotonicity of $\tan$. Then
$h(y)=y+y^3-\tan y$ has $h(0)=0$ and $h'(y)=3y^2-\tan^2y>3y^2-3y^2=0$.

\ref{E:atan}: apply $\tan$ to both sides for the identity. The condition $pq>-1$ keeps the
difference in $(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2)$. The inequality $\arctan z\le z$ holds since $\tan$ is
convex on $[0,\frac\pi2)$.

\ref{E:mono}: the derivative has numerator $1+S^2T^2+z^2>0$.
